stem: Which reagents convert benzene into chlorobenzene?

options.content: chlorine with an aluminium chloride catalyst
options.rationale: Correct: electrophilic substitution with a halogen carrier.

options.content: chlorine in ultraviolet light
options.rationale: UV light gives free-radical reactions, mainly addition to benzene, not chlorobenzene.

options.content: hydrogen chloride gas at room temperature
options.rationale: HCl does not substitute into the benzene ring.

options.content: aqueous sodium chloride with heating
options.rationale: Chloride ions are nucleophiles and do not attack the ring.

explanation: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → C₆H₅Cl + HCl (AlCl₃ catalyst).

stem: Why is chlorobenzene much less easily hydrolysed than chloroethane?

options.content: A chlorine lone pair overlaps with the ring's π system, strengthening the C–Cl bond.
options.rationale: Correct: partial double-bond character.

options.content: The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is more polar than in chloroethane.
options.rationale: Greater polarity would make attack easier, not harder.

options.content: Chlorobenzene does not dissolve in water at all, so no reaction is possible.
options.rationale: Insolubility alone is not the reason; it does not react even in ethanol solution.

options.content: Chlorine in chlorobenzene is present as a chloride ion, not covalently bonded.
options.rationale: Chlorine is covalently bonded to the ring.

explanation: Delocalisation of a Cl lone pair gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character.

stem: Which bond in dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl₂F₂, is broken by ultraviolet light in the stratosphere?

options.content: C–Cl, because it is weaker than C–F
options.rationale: Correct: the weakest bond breaks, releasing Cl•.

options.content: C–F, because it is the most polar bond
options.rationale: C–F is stronger than C–Cl and survives.

options.content: Cl–Cl, because chlorine atoms are joined together
options.rationale: There is no Cl–Cl bond in CCl₂F₂.

options.content: F–F, because fluorine is the most reactive halogen
options.rationale: There is no F–F bond in CCl₂F₂.

explanation: CCl₂F₂ → CClF₂• + Cl•.

stem: Poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE, is used to coat non-stick pans. Which property makes it suitable?

options.content: It reacts with food fats to form a protective layer.
options.rationale: PTFE does not react with food.

options.content: It is very unreactive and heat resistant, with a low-friction surface.
options.rationale: Correct: strong C–F bonds make it inert.

options.content: It conducts heat better than metals do.
options.rationale: PTFE is a poor conductor; the metal pan conducts heat.

options.content: It dissolves slowly to release lubricating fluorine gas.
options.rationale: PTFE is insoluble and releases no fluorine in normal use.

explanation: Inertness and heat resistance from strong C–F bonds.

stem: Which equation shows the step in which the chlorine radical is regenerated during ozone depletion?

options.rationale: This step uses up Cl• and destroys ozone.
Correct: Cl• is reformed, so it acts as a catalyst.

options.content: $\ce{CCl2F2 -> CClF2^. + Cl^.}$
options.rationale: This is photodissociation, which first forms Cl•.
This termination step removes radicals.

explanation: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ then ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂.
hints: Which step has Cl• as a product?

stem: Chlorobenzene and (chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, are each warmed with ethanolic silver nitrate. What is observed?

options.content: Both give a white precipitate at the same rate.
options.rationale: The C–Cl bond on the ring is not hydrolysed.

options.content: Chlorobenzene gives a white precipitate; (chloromethyl)benzene gives none.
options.rationale: This is the reverse of what happens.

options.content: Both give a yellow precipitate of silver chloride.
options.rationale: Silver chloride is white, and only one compound reacts.

options.content: (chloromethyl)benzene gives a white precipitate; chlorobenzene gives none.
options.rationale: Correct: the side-chain C–Cl is a normal halogenoalkane bond.

explanation: C₆H₅CH₂Cl behaves as a halogenoalkane; C₆H₅Cl does not react.
hints: Is the Cl attached to the ring or to the side chain?

stem: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of aluminium chloride, in the dark. What are the main organic products?

options.content: (chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, only
options.rationale: That forms in UV light without a catalyst.

options.rationale: –CH₃ is 2,4-directing.

options.rationale: The methyl group is not removed from the ring.

options.rationale: Correct: ring substitution directed by CH₃ to positions 2 and 4.

stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of chlorine in dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl₂F₂, to one decimal place. Ar: C 12.0, F 19.0, Cl 35.5.
In the stratosphere each CCl₂F₂ molecule first releases one chlorine radical. Calculate the number of chlorine radicals released by 5.00 g of CCl₂F₂ (Mr = 121.0; L = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).
explanation:
1. n(CCl₂F₂) = 5.00 ÷ 121.0 = 0.0413 mol.
2. Number of molecules = 0.0413 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.49 × 10²²; one Cl• each, so 2.49 × 10²² radicals.
3. Doubling (two Cl per molecule) ignores the statement that one radical is released at first.
workedSolution:
1. 1. n(CCl₂F₂) = 5.00 ÷ 121.0 = 0.0413 mol.
2. Number of molecules = 0.0413 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.49 × 10²²; one Cl• each, so 2.49 × 10²² radicals.
3. Doubling (two Cl per molecule) ignores the statement that one radical is released at first.
hints: Moles of CCl₂F₂ first, then multiply by L.

stem: Explain why chlorobenzene does not react with warm aqueous sodium hydroxide, although chloroethane does.

points.description: A lone pair on chlorine (in a p orbital) overlaps with / is delocalised into the ring's π system
This gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character, so it is stronger (and shorter) than in chloroethane and harder to break
The electron-rich π cloud also repels the OH⁻ nucleophile (and the carbon is less δ+)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: One of the chlorine's lone pairs overlaps with the delocalised π electrons of the ring, so the C–Cl bond has some double-bond character and is stronger than the C–Cl bond in chloroethane. The hydroxide ion is also repelled by the π electron cloud of the ring and cannot attack the carbon from behind, so no substitution occurs under these conditions.

explanation: Stronger bond and repulsion of nucleophiles.
hints: Lone pair, delocalisation, bond strength, repulsion.

stem: Describe, with equations, how CFCl₃ released at ground level leads to the destruction of ozone in the stratosphere.

points.description: CFCl₃ is inert, so it persists and diffuses up into the stratosphere
UV light breaks the weakest bond, C–Cl, homolytically: CFCl₃ → CFCl₂• + Cl•
ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂: Cl• regenerated, acting as a catalyst

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: CFCl₃ is so unreactive that it is not destroyed in the lower atmosphere and slowly rises into the stratosphere. There, ultraviolet radiation breaks a C–Cl bond: CFCl₃ → CFCl₂• + Cl•. The chlorine radical reacts with ozone, Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, and the ClO• reacts with an oxygen atom, ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. Cl• is regenerated, so it catalyses the destruction of many ozone molecules.

explanation: One mark per stage.

stem: Suggest why hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are not a perfect replacement for CFCs.

points.description: Many HFCs are powerful greenhouse gases, contributing to global warming
They are more expensive or less efficient in some uses, or some alternatives (hydrocarbons) are flammable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Although HFCs contain no chlorine and do not damage ozone, many absorb infrared radiation strongly and are potent greenhouse gases. Some alternatives such as hydrocarbons are flammable, and replacements can be more costly.

explanation: Any two valid points.
hints: Ozone is not the only environmental issue.
